paras: The Oconee Christmas Day riot was an armed clash on December 25, 1882, at Oconee, Georgia, between the town marshal, the mayor and white citizens and a group of Black men the marshal was trying to arrest. Three or four Black men were shot, one reportedly mortally, and the marshal and his son were wounded. A Macon wire sent across the country on December 30 called it a "race riot" that had killed a white man, but a second Macon dispatch the same day said no one had been killed.

According to a Sandersville dispatch, several Black men "under the influence of liquor" had become "very troublesome" on Saturday, December 23, and the town marshal, Webster, arrested one of them. The same dispatch said that on Monday they "returned armed", which the white citizens had not expected.

A Toomsboro dispatch said the marshal was resisted when he tried to arrest some Black men who were fighting, and that a general fight followed in which Mayor Snell and his sons and the marshal and his son took part. By this white account, the Black men fired first and hit the marshal's son, who then "put two bullets into a negro" who was not expected to live. The Sandersville report counted three Black men shot and said the marshal was seriously injured but "doing very well."

The later Macon dispatch named the Black men as the Washington brothers, "five in number", and said a Black man named Ira Lawson came to their aid while citizens joined the marshal. Knives and pistols were drawn on both sides, and it counted three whites and four Black men wounded, with only Lawson seriously hurt.

On Tuesday, after rumors that Black residents would try to rescue the prisoners, the whites sent to Toomsboro for help, and the marshal there came with a posse of ten. The Toomsboro dispatch reported that all was quiet; no report of an inquest, charges or trial was found.

Coverage came only from the white press, starting with brief Georgia dispatches in the Savannah Morning News, which put the riot in a column of "home Christmas tragedies" and blamed drunk and armed Black men. On December 30 a Macon wire ran in Washington, St. Paul, Memphis and, in German, Cincinnati under headings such as "RACE RIOT IN GEORGIA", reporting Asa Lawson killed and "Marshall Webster" and his son mortally wounded, "all white men." The names varied between papers, with the marshal's son given as "William", "Lon Williams" or "Leo Williams."

A second Macon dispatch, printed the next day by The Sun as "A Marshal Attacked by Negroes", by the Richmond Dispatch and by the New-York Tribune, said the riot report had grown out of a row with "a family of drunken negroes." It called Ira Lawson a "negro desperado" and presented the event as Black resistance to an arrest.

The first Macon wire said a white man named Asa Lawson was killed, while the later dispatch said Ira Lawson was Black, sided with the Washingtons and survived as the only person seriously hurt. Neither Georgia dispatch, both written within two days, reports a white death, and they and the later dispatch date the fight to Christmas Day rather than December 29 or 30. Every account comes from the white side; no statement from the Washington brothers or other Black witnesses was found.

reader.title: Oconee Christmas Day riot
bases: The town marshal's attempt to arrest Black men turned into a gunfight in which the marshal, his son, the mayor and his sons and other citizens shot several Black men (A1, A2, A7).

Georgia dispatches and both Macon wires agree that an armed clash took place at Oconee, but the first Macon wire reports a white man, Asa Lawson, killed (A3, A4), while the later Macon dispatch says the only person seriously hurt was a Black man, Ira Lawson, and reports no one killed (A7).

accounts.label: Sandersville and Toomsboro dispatches
accounts.gist: On Christmas Day, Black men, one of whom had been arrested on Saturday, resisted or fought the marshal; the marshal's son was shot and wounded a Black man mortally; the marshal was seriously injured, and whites called in a posse from Toomsboro.

accounts.label: First Macon wire
accounts.gist: A 'race riot' at Oconee killed Asa Lawson and mortally wounded Marshall Webster and his son, all white, and dangerously wounded three Washington brothers.

accounts.label: Later Macon dispatch
accounts.gist: A Christmas Day row between five drunken Washington brothers and the marshal was reported as a riot; citizens joined the marshal, Ira Lawson joined the brothers, seven were wounded, and only Lawson was seriously hurt.

framing.detail: Northern and western papers ran the first Macon wire under 'RACE RIOT IN GEORGIA', listing white dead and wounded first.

The Georgia dispatches and the later Macon dispatch placed the blame on Black men, calling them drunk and 'troublesome' and Ira Lawson a 'negro desperado', under the headline 'A Marshal Attacked by Negroes'.

conflicts.note: The dispatches from Sandersville and Toomsboro were written within two days of the fight, and the later Macon dispatch also says Christmas Day, so Dec. 25 is the better-supported date.
